title: How to practise here
summary: Why you type everything by hand, what each kind of task asks of you, and how reviews come back.

sections.heading: Why you type every character
body: Reading code feels like understanding it. Typing it is how your hands and head actually learn it. That is why paste, autocomplete and automatic closing brackets are all switched off.
Go slowly at first. Accuracy builds speed; speed does not build accuracy.

sections.heading: The six kinds of task
body: - **Solve**: write a function from scratch until every test passes.
- **Fix the bug**: the code almost works. Find the one small mistake.
- **Predict the output**: read the code, write down what it prints, then run it and compare.
- **Typing drill**: copy a snippet exactly. You get speed and accuracy, not tests.
- **Translate**: working code in one language, rewrite it in another.
- **Refactor**: the code works but is messy. Keep the tests green and meet the extra rules.

sections.heading: When you are stuck
body: Read the error first. It names the line, and the line is highlighted in the editor.
Look at one failing test: the input, what was expected, and what your code returned. `undefined` or `None` usually means a missing `return`.
Open the study notes linked under the task title. Hints are there too, but each hint you reveal brings the task back for review sooner.

sections.heading: How reviews come back
body: Every check is saved. The Today list on the home screen uses it to choose what to practise:
- Passed with hints: it comes back in 2 days.
- Passed without hints: it comes back in 7 days, and each clean pass after that doubles the wait.
